paragraphs: Once there was a miller with a beautiful daughter. Now that she was grown, he wanted her to be provided for and well married. “If a good suitor comes and asks for her,” he thought, “I will give her to him.” Not long afterwards, a suitor appeared who seemed very rich. The miller could find no fault with him, so he promised him his daughter. The girl, however, did not like him as much as a girl should like the man she is engaged to, and she did not trust him. Whenever she saw or thought of him, she felt a secret horror. Once he said to her, “You are engaged to me, yet you have never visited me.” “I don’t know where your house is,” she replied. “My house is out there in the dark forest,” the bridegroom said. She tried to excuse herself, saying she could not find the way. “You must come to me next Sunday,” he said. “I have already invited the guests. I will scatter ashes so that you can find your way through the forest.” When Sunday came and she had to set out, the girl felt very uneasy, though she did not quite know why. To mark her path, she filled both pockets with peas and lentils. Ashes had been scattered at the entrance to the forest, and she followed them, dropping a couple of peas on the ground at every step. She walked for almost the whole day before reaching the middle of the forest, where it was darkest. There stood a lonely house. She did not like it, for it looked so dark and gloomy. She went inside, but no one was there, and everything was utterly still. Suddenly a voice cried:

“Turn back, turn back, dear young girl,
You are entering a murderer’s house.”
The girl looked up and saw that the voice came from a bird in a cage hanging on the wall. Again it cried:

“Turn back, turn back, dear young girl,
You are entering a murderer’s house.”

The girl went farther, from room to room, through the whole house. It was completely empty, with not a single person to be found. At last she came to the cellar. There sat an extremely old woman whose head shook constantly. “Can you tell me,” the girl asked, “whether my fiancé lives here?”

“Oh, poor child,” the old woman replied, “where have you come? You are in a murderers’ den. You think you are a bride about to be married, but your wedding will be with death. Look, they have forced me to put that great kettle of water on the fire. When they have you in their power, they will cut you to pieces without mercy, cook you and eat you, for they eat human flesh. Unless I take pity on you and save you, you are lost.”

The old woman led her behind a great barrel, where she could not be seen. “Be as quiet as a mouse,” she said. “Do not make a sound or move, or it will be all over for you. Tonight, when the robbers are asleep, we will escape. I have waited a long time for a chance.” She had barely done this when the godless gang came home, dragging another young girl with them. They were drunk and paid no attention to her screams and cries. They gave her three full glasses of wine to drink: one of white wine, one of red, and one of yellow. At this, her heart burst in two. Then they tore off her delicate clothes, laid her on a table, cut her beautiful body into pieces, and scattered salt over them. The poor bride behind the barrel trembled and shook. She could see only too well the fate the robbers had planned for her. One of them noticed a gold ring on the murdered girl’s little finger. When it did not come off at once, he took an axe and cut off the finger. It flew into the air, over the barrel, and landed straight in the bride’s bosom. The robber took a candle and began searching for it, but could not find it. Another asked, “Have you looked behind the big barrel?” But the old woman called, “Come and get something to eat. Leave the search until morning—the finger won’t run away.”

“The old woman is right,” the robbers said. They stopped searching and sat down to eat. The old woman poured a sleeping potion into their wine, and soon they lay down in the cellar and slept and snored. When the bride heard this, she came out from behind the barrel. She had to step over the sleeping men, who lay in rows on the ground, and she was terrified of waking one of them. But God helped her, and she got across safely. The old woman went upstairs with her and opened the doors. They hurried out of the murderers’ den as fast as they could. The wind had blown away the ashes, but the peas and lentils had sprouted and grown, showing them the path in the moonlight. They walked all night and reached the mill in the morning. Then the girl told her father everything, exactly as it had happened.

When the wedding day came, the bridegroom arrived, and the miller had invited all his relatives and friends. As they sat at the table, everyone was asked to tell a story. The bride sat quietly and said nothing. Then the bridegroom said to her, “Come, my darling, don’t you know a story? Tell us something, like the others.” “Then I will tell you a dream,” she replied. “I was walking alone through a wood. At last I came to a house with not a living soul inside. But on the wall was a bird in a cage, and it cried:

“Turn back, turn back, dear young girl,
You are entering a murderer’s house.”

“And it cried the same thing once more. My darling, I only dreamed this. Then I went through all the rooms, and they were empty, and there was something so horrible about them! At last I went down to the cellar. There sat a very, very old woman whose head shook. I asked her, ‘Does my bridegroom live in this house?’ She answered, ‘Oh, poor child, you have come into a murderers’ den. Your bridegroom does live here, but he will cut you to pieces and kill you, then cook you and eat you.’ My darling, I only dreamed this. But the old woman hid me behind a great barrel. I had barely hidden when the robbers came home, dragging a girl with them. They gave her three kinds of wine to drink—white, red and yellow—and her heart broke in two. My darling, I only dreamed this. Then they pulled off her pretty clothes, cut her beautiful body into pieces on a table, and sprinkled them with salt. My darling, I only dreamed this. One of the robbers saw that there was still a ring on her little finger. It was hard to pull off, so he took an axe and cut the finger off. But the finger flew into the air, over the great barrel, and fell into my bosom. And here is the finger with the ring!” With these words she brought it out and showed everyone there.

The robber had grown as pale as ash during the story. He jumped up and tried to escape, but the guests held him fast and handed him over to the authorities. Then he and his whole gang were executed for their infamous deeds.
